descriptive_title: Grade 1 Mathematics: Numbers — Reading, Composing, Comparing, Counting, and Sharing Numbers to 50, with Halves and Fourths (B1.1–B1.8)
subject: Mathematics

curriculum_expectations.B1.1: read and represent whole numbers up to and including 50, and describe various ways they are used in everyday life
curriculum_expectations.B1.2: compose and decompose whole numbers up to and including 50, using a variety of tools and strategies, in various contexts
curriculum_expectations.B1.3: compare and order whole numbers up to and including 50, in various contexts
curriculum_expectations.B1.4: estimate the number of objects in collections of up to 50, and verify their estimates by counting
curriculum_expectations.B1.5: count to 50 by 1s, 2s, 5s, and 10s, using a variety of tools and strategies
curriculum_expectations.B1.6: use drawings to represent and solve fair-share problems that involve 2 and 4 sharers, respectively, and have remainders of 1 or 2
curriculum_expectations.B1.7: recognize that one half and two fourths of the same whole are equal, in fair-sharing contexts
curriculum_expectations.B1.8: use drawings to compare and order unit fractions representing the individual portions that result when a whole is shared by different numbers of sharers, up to a maximum of 10

unit_overview: A 5-day Grade 1 unit on Numbers framed around 'Number Friends to 50' — Lila the Button Collector, Otto the Marble Counter, and Scoot the friendly puppy mascot who cheers them on. Children begin Day 1 by estimating Lila's button jar and counting collections to 50 by 1s, 2s, 5s, and 10s (B1.4, B1.5). Day 2 focuses on reading and representing numbers to 50 in many forms — numerals, words, ten-frame fills, base-ten rods, tally marks, and real-life uses (B1.1). Day 3 is the keystone: composing and decomposing numbers to 50 with multiple strategies — partition into tens and ones, partner-pair flexible decomp, breaking apart for easier addition (B1.2). Day 4 brings comparison and ordering of numbers to 50 with the Number Line classroom and a range of compare-the-collection scenarios (B1.3). Day 5 closes with fair-sharing problems for 2 and 4 sharers (B1.6) and the unit-fraction reveal: half = two fourths (B1.7), with comparison of unit fractions up to tenths (B1.8). The unit moves from concrete (real buttons, marbles, base-ten rods) to representational (ten-frames, number lines, sharing diagrams) to abstract (numerical comparison, fraction notation).
unit_learning_goal: Children will read, represent, compose, decompose, compare, order, estimate, and count whole numbers to 50, share collections fairly between 2 and 4 sharers, and recognise that one half equals two fourths of the same whole.

lesson_arc.big_idea: We can count by 1s, 2s, 5s, and 10s. Bigger groups need smarter counting strategies.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can estimate how many in a collection up to 50, and count by 1s, 2s, 5s, and 10s to check.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Lila's button jar estimation challenge; whole-class skip-counting on the Number Line by 1s, 2s, 5s, 10s; partner verification with real collections.

lesson_arc.big_idea: The same number can be shown many ways. Numerals, words, tally marks, ten-frames, and base-ten rods all mean the same amount.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can read and represent numbers to 50 in many ways and tell where I see numbers in everyday life.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Number Friends gallery walk: each station shows a number 0-50 in 5 different forms; children rotate through and match. Real-life number hunt around the classroom.

lesson_arc.big_idea: Numbers can be split into tens and ones, or into other partner pairs. Different splits help with different problems.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can compose and decompose any number to 50 using tens, ones, and partner pairs in different ways.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Base-ten rod decomposition; partner-pair Make-the-Number game; flexible decomposition (e.g. 32 = 10+10+10+2 = 25+7 = 30+2). Keystone lesson with the side-by-side comparison of decompositions.

lesson_arc.big_idea: We compare numbers by looking at their tens and ones. We order numbers from smallest to biggest using the Number Line.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can compare two numbers up to 50 and order a small set from smallest to biggest.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Compare-the-Jar partner activity (which jar has more?); Number Line ordering with sticky-note number cards; partner debate over close numbers (37 vs 41).

lesson_arc.big_idea: Sharing fairly between 2 friends gives halves; between 4 friends gives fourths. One half equals two fourths of the same thing.
lesson_arc.student_learning_goal: I can share a small collection fairly between 2 or 4 friends, draw the share, and tell that one half equals two fourths.
lesson_arc.one_line_summary: Fair-share rounds with 2 and 4 sharers (with leftovers of 1 or 2); pizza-slice fraction reveal showing 1/2 = 2/4; ordering unit fractions 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest.

recurring_characters.name: Lila
recurring_characters.role: Lead Number Friend — collects buttons; runs the estimation jar in Lesson 1 and demonstrates the gallery walk in Lesson 2.
recurring_characters.visual_description: A young Grade-1er with bright orange overalls and a button-collection apron pinned with colourful buttons. Light brown hair in a single side ponytail, friendly smile, holding a clear glass jar of buttons.

recurring_characters.name: Otto
recurring_characters.role: Lila's pair partner — collects marbles in jars; models compare-the-jar in Lesson 4 and base-ten decomposition in Lesson 3.
recurring_characters.visual_description: A young Grade-1er with a green plaid shirt and rolled-up jeans, dark curly hair, warm grin, holding two jars of marbles (red and blue) side by side.

recurring_characters.name: Scoot
recurring_characters.role: Number Friend mascot — a friendly puppy who appears in every lesson with a 'how many' speech bubble. The unit's counting cheerleader.
recurring_characters.visual_description: A small smiling puppy (golden retriever style) with a red collar and a small bandana with the word COUNT printed on it. Drawn standing alertly, big eyes, friendly tail-wag.

threaded_vocabulary.child_friendly_definition: make a smart guess about how many — close, but not exact yet.
put two or more numbers together to make a bigger number.
break a bigger number apart into smaller pieces that add up to it.
look at two numbers and decide which is bigger, smaller, or equal.
put a list of numbers in line from smallest to biggest (or biggest to smallest).
every number to 50 has tens (groups of 10) and ones (single units). 32 has 3 tens and 2 ones.
give the same amount to every person; check that all shares are equal.
what is left over when a fair share doesn't come out even.
a half is one of two equal shares; a fourth is one of four equal shares of the same thing.
a fraction that names ONE share of a whole — like 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5.

manipulatives_index.name: Lila's Button Set
manipulatives_index.description: Per-pair set of 50 small printed button cards in 5 colours (10 each). Used for Lesson 1 estimation and counting, Lesson 3 base-ten decomposition, Lesson 4 compare-the-jar.

manipulatives_index.name: Estimation Button Jar
manipulatives_index.description: Clear jar holding 35-50 buttons. Used in Lesson 1 for the estimate-then-count routine; revisited in Lesson 4 for compare-the-jar.

manipulatives_index.name: Base-Ten Rods
manipulatives_index.description: Per-child set: 5 ten-rods (10 ones each, total 50) and 20 single ones. Used for Lesson 2 representations and Lesson 3 compose/decompose work.

manipulatives_index.name: Number Line Floor Mat
manipulatives_index.description: Long printable floor strip showing numbers 0 to 50 with cells ~6in each. Children walk the Number Line in Lesson 1 (skip-counting) and Lesson 4 (ordering and comparing).

manipulatives_index.name: Fair-Share Pizza Cards
manipulatives_index.description: Printable letter-size cards showing whole pizzas, halves, and fourths. Used in Lesson 5 to reveal that 1/2 = 2/4 visually.

manipulatives_index.name: Sharing Paper Plates
manipulatives_index.description: Set of 4 paper plates per group. Children deal collections fairly between 2 sharers and 4 sharers in Lesson 5.

manipulatives_index.name: Number-Word Match Cards
manipulatives_index.description: Per-pair set of 30 cards: 10 numerals (5, 12, 25, 38, 50, etc.) + 10 number words (five, twelve, twenty-five, etc.) + 10 representation cards (ten-frames, base-ten rods, tally marks). Used in Lesson 2 gallery walk.

materials_overview: Button collection per pair: ~50 printed button cards in 5 colours (or real buttons)
Base-ten rods: 5 ten-rods + 20 single ones per child
Number Line floor mat (0 to 50, ~25ft long)
Paper plates (4 per group of 4 children)
Anchor chart 'Tens and Ones' with 5 rows showing 10/20/30/40/50 as base-ten visuals
Sticky notes for child names and number cards on the floor Number Line

assessment_strategy.diagnostic: Lesson 1 estimate-vs-count: record each child's estimate of buttons in the jar and the actual count. Children whose estimate is within 5 of actual show emerging quantity-sense at scale. Children with gaps over 10 may need anchor-counting practice during Day 2 small groups.
assessment_strategy.formative: Lesson 2 representations tracker: tally per child which 5 forms (numeral, word, ten-frame, base-ten rod, tally) they can independently produce for a given target number. Lesson 3 decomposition observation: can the child produce ≥2 different decompositions for the same number? Lesson 4 compare-the-jar: can the child compare two jars without recounting from scratch?
assessment_strategy.summative: Lesson 5 Fair-Share + Fraction worksheet — three priced share scenarios + a unit-fraction comparison; child draws and labels the share, then orders 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 from largest to smallest. Captures B1.6, B1.7, B1.8 explicitly and pulls in B1.3 implicitly.

pedagogical_notes: B1.5 says 'count to 50 by 1s, 2s, 5s, 10s' — the difficult counts in Grade 1 are 2s and 5s starting from a non-multiple (e.g. 'count by 5s starting at 17'). Plan to do this in Lesson 1's stretch.
B1.7 'one half = two fourths' is conceptually subtle. Use the same circular pizza in both halved and fourthed states; physically overlay the half-piece onto the two fourth-pieces to show equivalence.

B1.8 (compare unit fractions) has a counter-intuitive rule: bigger denominator = SMALLER share. Children intuit 'bigger number = bigger thing' (consistent with their whole-number experience). The repair is to show that more sharers means smaller pieces.

Composition and decomposition (B1.2) is the keystone — children need to flexibly see 32 as 30+2 AND 25+7 AND 10+10+10+2. The single-strategy child is operationally weak; build multi-strategy fluency in Lesson 3 small groups.
Differentiate: students confident with numbers to 50 should get extension cards reaching to 100 in Lesson 4 ordering, and 1/6 / 1/8 / 1/10 unit fractions in Lesson 5 comparison.

Estimation accuracy at scale (B1.4 to 50) requires a 'chunking' strategy — count one group of 10 first, then estimate 'about how many groups like that'. Without this strategy, K-style guesswork dominates.
canadian_context_notes: Lila's button collection is intentionally diverse — buttons of different shapes, sizes, and patterns (some sewn, some snap, some toggle) reflecting real Canadian classroom button-jars. Multilingual classrooms can label buttons in students' home languages.
Pizza is the canonical fair-share example for halves and fourths. Schools running halal or kosher snack policies can swap to butter tarts (halved) or naan (quartered) as cultural variations.
Number-Word Match Cards include both English and FSL number words for FSL classrooms (a teacher option, not required for the base unit).
Scoot the puppy mascot's 'COUNT' bandana can be re-labelled in any classroom language; the visual remains the same.
